conversation.content:
Good morning, [preferred name]. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you. We’ll use a short tool called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to understand what emotional support might help you most right now.

Everything you share stays confidential within our team unless safety is a concern; then we work together to keep you safe. The EPDS has 10 questions about the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and you can pause or ask for clarification at any time.

Ready to begin? First, I’d love to know: Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that spark felt harder to find?

[pauses, eyes a little watery]

It’s… mostly harder. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the morning light coming through the blinds—something that used to feel peaceful—and I think, “That’s pretty,” but the warm feeling is… dim, like the color’s been turned down. I still smile when my toddler sings the alphabet wrong, but even that fades fast and I’m left tired and flat again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’ve laughed a little—like when my mom sent that silly video of the dog—but it feels forced and disappears right away. Most of the time I can’t really find the funny side, even when I know something’s supposed to be humorous.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I used to get excited about simple stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now when I think about those things it just feels kind of empty, like “what’s the point?” I still do them because I know I should, but the happy anticipation isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for an hour and I kept thinking it must be because I’m not soothing him right, or I ate something that upset my milk. Even when my toddler spilled juice I caught myself thinking, “If I were a better mom I’d have put the cup farther back.” I know it’s not all my fault, but the guilty thoughts just pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet—what if he stopped breathing? I check him over and over, even when I know he’s fine. The worries jump from one thing to the next: the outlet covers, the dog’s nails near his face, whether I sterilized the bottle right. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry while the baby napped, and suddenly my chest felt tight, like I couldn’t get enough air. My heart was pounding and I thought, “Something awful is about to happen,” even though nothing was wrong. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding just when I finally sit down to eat, my toddler drops the crackers on the floor and I want to cry. I keep thinking, “I can’t do this,” but I push through because I have to. It’s exhausting.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down and my head just keeps spinning with everything I didn’t do right or might forget tomorrow. Some nights it takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and then I jerk awake worrying the baby’s blanket moved over his face. I probably wake up two times like that before morning, heart racing, even when he’s still sound asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I’ll be nursing the baby and tears just start leaking—no real reason. It’s like there’s this heavy gray blanket over everything. I wouldn’t say it’s every single minute, but most parts of the day feel… sad, and when people ask how I am, the first word that pops into my head is “miserable.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week it got that bad. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t latch and I just sat there in the rocker with tears streaming down, couldn’t stop for maybe ten minutes. And then a couple days before that my partner asked what was wrong and the words wouldn’t come out—just crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…yes. Just fleeting things, like when I’m really overwhelmed at 3 a.m.—the idea pops in that maybe everyone would be better off if I just weren’t here. I’ve never planned anything; it’s more like a scary flash that I immediately push away because I could never leave my kids. But it’s happened once or twice this week and it frightens me.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note

Symptoms / behavioral concerns endorsed
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt / self-blame (parenting, infant care)  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-if” worries, panic-type episode  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty coping with daily tasks  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan or intent)

Patterns
Consistent across items: mood, anxiety, guilt, and functional impairment cluster together; symptoms present “most days” and worsen at night.

Screening significance
- Meets clinical threshold concern for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset (PHQ-9 equivalent ≥ moderate)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 equivalent moderate–severe)  
- Safety: presence of self-harm thoughts warrants immediate risk assessment

Risk factors highlighted
- Passive suicidal ideation (safety priority)  
- Sleep deprivation amplifying mood liability  
- Infant care stressors intensifying guilt / anxiety loop  
- No reported protective factors (support utilization, respite) at this time

Observation
Client is a postpartum mother reporting multiple depressive and anxious symptoms of ≥2-week duration, with associated impairment in functioning and fleeting suicidal thoughts. Recommend expedited referral for comprehensive clinical evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options including therapy, medication, and enhanced support services.
